教育竊有志乎聖賢之學其於參賛之功家相之事雖
不敢與聞而所得於天以生之理為心之所固有者
固不容諉於不知矣敢不援經摭史為
陛下陳之臣惟天子父天母地而為之子云者此漢儒班
固之言也大君者吾父母宗子云者此宋儒張載之
punctuated:
今日之欲比隆前古者，蓋必有說矣。洪惟皇帝陛下，鍾天地之粹氣，禀天地之全德，以撫有普天率土之人民。臨御以来，勵精圖治，凡可以當天心、慰人望者，無所不用其極，誠可謂大有為之君，可謂善繼述之宗子矣。然乃不自滿足，首進臣等於廷，詢之以父母宗子之責，且謂儒者之道，以位天地、育萬物、參天地、賛化育為極至，而求行之之序所自始焉。臣有以見陛下之心，真知儒道之至重，深圖君責之惟艱，直欲無一念之愧乎天，無一事之愧乎古，無一制度、無一政令之不得其宜，無一民一物之不被其澤而後已。顧臣愚昧，何足以知之？然於乾坤之間，得與胞與之列，厠名為儒，久荷教育，竊有志乎聖賢之學。其於參賛之功、冢相之事，雖不敢與聞，而所得於天以生之理，為心之所固有者，固不容諉於不知矣。敢不援經擿史，為陛下陳之？
臣惟「天子父天母地而為之子」云者，此漢儒班固之言也。「大君者吾父母宗子」云者，此宋儒張載之
translation_en:
…and the present aspiration to rival the flourishing achievements of antiquity must surely have an explanation. Reverently considering Your Majesty the Emperor: you embody the purest vital energy of Heaven and Earth and are endowed with their complete virtue, that you may rule and nurture the people everywhere beneath Heaven and throughout the land. Since ascending the throne, you have devoted your energies to good government, exerting yourself to the utmost in everything that might accord with Heaven’s heart and satisfy the people’s hopes. Truly, you may be called a ruler of great accomplishment and a lineage heir who ably carries forward his forebears’ intentions and undertakings. Yet you have not rested content. You have first summoned us, your servants, to court and questioned us about the responsibilities of a parent and a lineage heir. Moreover, you have said that the Confucian Way reaches its highest fulfillment in bringing Heaven and Earth into their proper positions, nurturing the myriad things, forming a triad with Heaven and Earth, and assisting their transforming and nurturing work; and you seek the starting point in the sequence of putting this into practice. From this I can see that Your Majesty truly understands the utmost importance of the Confucian Way and deeply considers the difficulty of a ruler’s responsibilities. You desire nothing less than to have no thought that would bring shame before Heaven, no deed that would bring shame before antiquity, no institution or governmental command that fails to be fitting, and no person or thing that does not receive your beneficence; only then will you rest. Yet how could your ignorant servant be adequate to understand this? Still, between Heaven and Earth, I have been granted a place among those regarded as siblings and companions, and count myself among the Confucian scholars. Long the recipient of your instruction and nurture, I have privately aspired to the learning of the sages and worthies. Although I dare not claim a part in the work of assisting Heaven and Earth or in the affairs of the chief minister, I cannot plead ignorance of the principle received from Heaven at birth, which is inherently present in my heart. How could I fail to cite the Classics and select evidence from the histories to set forth before Your Majesty?
Your servant considers that the statement, “The Son of Heaven takes Heaven as his father and Earth as his mother and is their son,” is a saying of the Han Confucian scholar Ban Gu. The statement, “The great ruler is the lineage heir of our father and mother,” is the Song Confucian scholar Zhang Zai’s…

title: 弘治三年進士登科錄
text:
言也蓋天下之理未嘗不一而天下之分未嘗不殊
故自天地而言則君為天之子對民物而言則君又
為天地之宗子獨不觀諸家乎一家之中凡繼其祖
者均得稱為宗凡繼其禰者均得稱為子惟宗子則
上承宗祧下合宗族而獨得謂之宗子故冠婚必告
之而莫敢專祭祀必主之而莫敢僭富貴必遜之而
莫敢加豈故以是而尊宗子哉誠以父母所遺之體
賴宗子以養父母所遺之業賴宗子以教宗子之所
在即父母之所在自不得不以父母尊之也天下之
眾凡稟氣於天者均得父稱乎天凡賦形於地者均
===
得母稱乎地惟大君則繼承天地統理民物而獨得
為天地之宗子故謂其所居之位曰天位謂其所享
之祿曰天祿謂其所都之邑曰天邑亦豈故以是而
尊大君哉誠以天地所與之形賴大君以養天地所
與之性賴大君以教大君之所在即天地之所在自
不得不以天地尊之也向使為家之宗子者不能教
養乎家而家之人有不得其所則一家得以尤之而
宗子何以逃其責於父母哉為天地之宗子者不能
教養乎天下而天下之人有不得其所則天下得以
望之而天子亦何以辭其責於天地哉試以唐虞三

之禄曰天禄謂其所都之邑曰天邑亦豈故以是而

punctuated: 言也。蓋天下之理未嘗不一，而天下之分未嘗不殊。故自天地而言，則君為天之子；對民物而言，則君又為天地之宗子。獨不觀諸家乎？一家之中，凡繼其祖者，均得稱為宗；凡繼其禰者，均得稱為子。惟宗子則上承宗祧，下合宗族，而獨得謂之宗子。故冠婚必告之，而莫敢專；祭祀必主之，而莫敢僭；富貴必遜之，而莫敢加。豈故以是而尊宗子哉？誠以父母所遺之體，賴宗子以養；父母所遺之業，賴宗子以教。宗子之所在，即父母之所在，自不得不以父母尊之也。天下之眾，凡稟氣於天者，均得父稱乎天；凡賦形於地者，均得母稱乎地。惟大君則繼承天地，統理民物，而獨得為天地之宗子。故謂其所居之位曰天位，謂其所享之祿曰天祿，謂其所都之邑曰天邑。亦豈故以是而尊大君哉？誠以天地所與之形，賴大君以養；天地所與之性，賴大君以教。大君之所在，即天地之所在，自不得不以天地尊之也。向使為家之宗子者不能教養乎家，而家之人有不得其所，則一家得以尤之，而宗子何以逃其責於父母哉？為天地之宗子者不能教養乎天下，而天下之人有不得其所，則天下得以望之，而天子亦何以辭其責於天地哉？試以唐虞三
translation_en:
…were his words. The principle underlying all under Heaven has always been one, yet the distinctions of station within it have always differed. Thus, viewed in relation to Heaven and Earth, the ruler is Heaven’s son; viewed in relation to the people and all other beings, he is also the principal lineage heir of Heaven and Earth. Have we not observed this in families? Within a family, whoever succeeds to his grandfather’s line may be called a lineage head, and whoever succeeds to his deceased father may be called a son. But the principal lineage heir alone carries on the ancestral succession above and unites the lineage below, and thus alone bears that designation. Accordingly, cappings and marriages must be reported to him, and none dares act independently; he must preside over sacrifices, and none dares usurp that role; in wealth and rank, all must yield precedence to him, and none dares place himself above him. Is this a contrivance to exalt the principal lineage heir? It is truly because the bodies bequeathed by the parents depend upon him for nurture, and the pursuits bequeathed by the parents depend upon him for instruction. Where the principal lineage heir is, there the parents are present; one therefore cannot but honor him as one honors the parents.

Among the multitudes under Heaven, all who receive vital energy from Heaven may call Heaven their father, and all who receive bodily form from Earth may call Earth their mother. But the sovereign alone succeeds Heaven and Earth and governs the people and all other beings together, and thus alone may be the principal lineage heir of Heaven and Earth. Hence the position he occupies is called the heavenly position, the emoluments he enjoys are called heavenly emoluments, and the city in which he establishes his capital is called the heavenly city. Is this, too, a contrivance to exalt the sovereign? It is truly because the bodily forms bestowed by Heaven and Earth depend upon the sovereign for nurture, and the natures bestowed by Heaven and Earth depend upon him for instruction. Where the sovereign is, there Heaven and Earth are present; one therefore cannot but honor him as one honors Heaven and Earth.

Suppose the principal lineage heir of a family were unable to instruct and nurture that family, so that some of its members failed to find their proper place: the whole family would have grounds to blame him. How could he escape his responsibility to the parents? If the principal lineage heir of Heaven and Earth cannot instruct and nurture all under Heaven, so that some people fail to find their proper place, then all under Heaven have grounds to reproach him. How, then, could the Son of Heaven disclaim his responsibility to Heaven and Earth? Let us consider those who ruled all under Heaven in the eras of Tang and Yu and the Three…

title: 弘治三年進士登科錄
text:
代之君天下者言之其養民則敬授人時播時百穀
六府孔脩輯寧邦家大賚四海也其教民則協和萬
邦慎徽五典文命四敷克綏厥猷重民五教也其為
治效則或賛其如天或美其風動或稱其天迪或以
為格于皇天或以為配天其澤也其於代天之功皆
能大有所為而宗子之責無不盡也以漢唐宋之君
天下者言之其養民則有籍田代田之詔有口分世
業之法民籍以定經界以均其教民則石渠白虎之
講說弘文廣文之招延博學宏詞之有試看詳學制
之有議其為治效則或雜伯或雜夷或偏安不振不
===
盡民力者不能免向隅之泣與民休息者不能免徭
役之勞寬厚待民者不能免閭里之怨嘆尊師重傳
而徒事乎章句訓詁之文大召名儒而無以變風雲
月露之態崇尚理學而無以革詞賦浮靡之習其於
代天之功雖或有所為而宗子之責則不能以皆盡
也夫其為宗子之責本同為治之制度政令亦畧同
而治效所至乃若是懸絕者豈世道之降端使然哉
臣嘗求其故矣曰欽明文思曰濬哲文明曰克勤克
儉曰克寛克仁曰執競維烈此其心純乎天天地民
物皆其度內所以立制度行政令而教養乎天下者

邦愼徽五典敷文命四敎克綏厥猷重民五敎也其爲
治效則或賛其如天或美其風動或稱其天廸或以
爲格于皇天或以爲配天其澤也其於代天之功皆

業之法民籍以定經界以均其教民則石渠白虎之
講說弘文廣文之招延博學宏詞之有試看詳學制
之有議其爲治效則或雜伯或雜夷或偏安不振不
===

役之勞寛厚待民者不能免閭里之怨嘆尊師重傳

也夫其爲宗子之責本同爲治之制度政令亦畧同
而治效所至乃若是懸絶者豈世道之降端使然哉
臣嘗求其故矣曰欽明文思曰濬哲文明曰克勤克
儉曰克寛克仁曰執競維烈此其心純乎天天地民
物皆其度內所以立制度行政令而教養乎天下者
punctuated:
代之君天下者言之，其養民則敬授人時，播時百穀，六府孔脩，輯寧邦家，大賚四海也。其教民則協和萬邦，慎徽五典，文命四敷，克綏厥猷，重民五教也。其為治效，則或賛其如天，或美其風動，或稱其天迪，或以為格于皇天，或以為配天其澤也。其於代天之功，皆能大有所為，而宗子之責無不盡也。
以漢唐宋之君天下者言之，其養民則有籍田代田之詔，有口分世業之法，民籍以定，經界以均。其教民則石渠白虎之講說，弘文廣文之招延，博學宏詞之有試，看詳學制之有議。其為治效，則或雜伯，或雜夷，或偏安不振。不盡民力者，不能免向隅之泣；與民休息者，不能免徭役之勞；寬厚待民者，不能免閭里之怨嘆。尊師重傳，而徒事乎章句訓詁之文；大召名儒，而無以變風雲月露之態；崇尚理學，而無以革詞賦浮靡之習。其於代天之功，雖或有所為，而宗子之責則不能以皆盡也。
夫其為宗子之責本同，為治之制度政令亦畧同，而治效所至乃若是懸絕者，豈世道之降端使然哉？臣嘗求其故矣。曰欽明文思，曰濬哲文明，曰克勤克儉，曰克寛克仁，曰執競維烈，此其心純乎天，天地民物皆其度內，所以立制度、行政令而教養乎天下者
translation_en:
…and the Three Dynasties, considering those who ruled All under Heaven: in nourishing the people, they reverently made known the seasons for human labor, sowed the various grains, brought the six resources into good order, secured peace for their states and houses, and bestowed great bounty throughout the Four Seas. In teaching the people, they harmonized the myriad states, carefully promoted the five constant duties, spread their civilizing instruction in all directions, firmly established the proper way, and attached importance to the five teachings for the people. As for the results of their government, some were praised as resembling Heaven; some were commended for transforming people as the wind moves things; some were said to be guided by Heaven; some were considered to have reached August Heaven; and some were held to match Heaven in their beneficence. In acting on Heaven’s behalf, all accomplished great things and fully discharged their responsibility as the principal heir.
Consider those who ruled All under Heaven during the Han, Tang, and Song. To nourish the people, they issued edicts on the imperial plowing field and the alternating-field method, and established rules for individual allotments and hereditary holdings. Population registers were settled and land boundaries equitably laid out. To teach the people, they held scholarly discussions at Shiqu and Baihu, recruited scholars to the Hongwen and Guangwen colleges, conducted examinations in broad learning and literary distinction, and deliberated on reviewing educational regulations. Yet the results of their government were sometimes mixed with the methods of hegemons, sometimes with foreign ways, or amounted to holding only part of the realm without recovering their strength. Those who refrained from exhausting the people’s strength could not prevent some from weeping neglected in a corner; those who allowed the people rest and recuperation could not spare them the toil of corvée service; those who treated the people generously could not prevent grievances and sighs in the villages. They honored teachers and valued transmitted learning, yet occupied themselves merely with textual divisions and explanations of words. They summoned eminent Confucian scholars in great numbers, yet could not change the literary manner that dwelt on wind and clouds, moonlight and dew. They esteemed the Learning of Principle, yet could not reform the frivolous and ornate habits of verse and rhapsody. Although they accomplished something in acting on Heaven’s behalf, they could not fully discharge their responsibility as the principal heir.
Their responsibility as the principal heir was fundamentally the same, and their governing institutions and administrative commands were also broadly similar. Why, then, were the results of their government so vastly different? Could the decline of the times alone have caused this? Your servant has sought the reason. It lies in the descriptions: “reverent, discerning, accomplished, and thoughtful”; “profoundly wise and brilliantly cultured”; “capable of diligence and frugality”; “capable of generosity and benevolence”; and “steadfast in strength, illustrious in achievement.” Their hearts were wholly attuned to Heaven; Heaven and Earth, the people and all things, lay within their concern. Thus, their establishment of institutions and implementation of administrative commands to teach and nourish All under Heaven…

title: 弘治三年進士登科錄
text:
皆心之所為用也或恭儉是尚而學宗黃老或儒術
是尚而性多褊察欲行仁義者大倫或已虧仁厚有
餘者剛斷或不足則其心為私欲所雜而不知民胞
物與之義雖有制度之立政令之行不過虛文美觀
以為教養之具惡能盡其心之用哉若夫位天地育
萬物參天地贊化育云者此則子思之言而亦張載
之意也蓋人之一身與天地並立而為三才雖有高
下大小之不同而理氣之貫通者未嘗有間吾之心
正則天地之心亦正而天地位吾之氣順則天地之
氣亦順而萬物育吾能位天地育萬物則化育之大
===
吾得而贊之天地之高厚吾得而參之儒者之道必
極於此而後可以為人君必極於此而後可以為君
可以為宗子也唐虞三代能盡宗子之責者此也漢
唐宋有宗子之責而未盡者則未極於此也然此豈
可以矯偽為亦豈可以旦夕致哉必自戒懼而約之
以至於至靜之中無少偏倚而其守不失則有以致
吾心之中而天地之所由以位也自慎獨而精之以
至於應物之際無少差謬而無適不然則有以致吾
心之和而萬物之所由以育也張載亦曰存心養性
為匪懈即戒懼之事也曰不愧屋漏為無忝即慎獨

氣亦順而萬物育吾能位天地育萬物則化育之大
===

心之和而萬物之所由以育也張載亦曰存心養性
為匪懈即戒懼之事也曰不愧屋漏為無忝即慎獨
punctuated:
皆心之所為用也。或恭儉是尚，而學宗黃老；或儒術是尚，而性多褊察；欲行仁義者，大倫或已虧；仁厚有餘者，剛斷或不足。則其心為私欲所雜，而不知民胞物與之義。雖有制度之立、政令之行，不過虛文美觀，以為教養之具，惡能盡其心之用哉？若夫位天地、育萬物、參天地、贊化育云者，此則子思之言，而亦張載之意也。蓋人之一身，與天地並立而為三才，雖有高下大小之不同，而理氣之貫通者，未嘗有間。吾之心正，則天地之心亦正，而天地位；吾之氣順，則天地之氣亦順，而萬物育。吾能位天地、育萬物，則化育之大，吾得而贊之；天地之高厚，吾得而參之。儒者之道，必極於此而後可以為人君，必極於此而後可以為君，可以為宗子也。唐虞三代能盡宗子之責者，此也；漢唐宋有宗子之責而未盡者，則未極於此也。

然此豈可以矯偽為，亦豈可以旦夕致哉？必自戒懼而約之，以至於至靜之中無少偏倚，而其守不失，則有以致吾心之中，而天地之所由以位也。自慎獨而精之，以至於應物之際無少差謬，而無適不然，則有以致吾心之和，而萬物之所由以育也。張載亦曰：「存心養性為匪懈。」即戒懼之事也。曰：「不愧屋漏為無忝。」即慎獨
translation_en:
…all are expressions of the functioning of the heart. Some esteemed reverence and frugality, yet in their learning followed the teachings of Huangdi and Laozi; some esteemed Confucian learning, yet were narrow-minded and excessively scrutinizing by disposition. Those who wished to practice benevolence and righteousness may already have impaired the cardinal human relationships; those abundant in benevolence and generosity may have lacked firmness and decisiveness. Their hearts were thus adulterated by selfish desires, and they did not understand the meaning of regarding the people as one's siblings and all things as one's companions. Although they established institutions and put administrative commands into effect, these amounted merely to empty forms and attractive appearances serving as instruments of instruction and nurture. How could they fully realize the functioning of their hearts?

As for bringing Heaven and Earth into their proper positions, nurturing the myriad things, forming a triad with Heaven and Earth, and assisting their transforming and nurturing activity: these are Zisi's words, and also Zhang Zai's meaning. The human person stands alongside Heaven and Earth to constitute the Three Powers. Although they differ in elevation and magnitude, there is never any interruption in the principle and vital energy that run through them. When my heart is correct, the heart of Heaven and Earth is likewise correct, and Heaven and Earth take their proper positions. When my vital energy is harmonious, the vital energy of Heaven and Earth is likewise harmonious, and the myriad things are nurtured. If I can bring Heaven and Earth into their proper positions and nurture the myriad things, I can assist the greatness of their transforming and nurturing activity; I can stand as a third alongside Heaven's height and Earth's depth. Only after carrying the Confucian Way to this utmost point can one become a ruler of men; only after carrying it to this utmost point can one become a ruler and serve as the principal lineage son. This is how the rulers of Tang and Yu and the Three Dynasties fulfilled their responsibility as principal lineage sons. The rulers of Han, Tang, and Song bore that responsibility but did not fulfill it because they had not reached this utmost point.

Yet how could this be accomplished through pretense, or attained overnight? One must begin with vigilance and apprehension and exercise self-restraint, until, in the utmost stillness, there is not the slightest deviation or inclination and one's self-command is never lost. One thereby brings the equilibrium of one's heart to its fullest realization, and through this Heaven and Earth take their proper positions. Beginning with watchfulness over oneself when alone, one must refine this practice until, in responding to things, there is not the slightest error, and this holds true in every circumstance. One thereby brings the harmony of one's heart to its fullest realization, and through this the myriad things are nurtured. Zhang Zai also said, “Preserving one's heart and nurturing one's nature constitute being unremitting.” This is precisely the work of vigilance and apprehension. He said, “Having nothing to be ashamed of even in the secluded recesses of one's room constitutes bringing no dishonor.” This is precisely watchfulness over oneself when alone…

title: 弘治三年進士登科錄
text:
之事也此欲盡宗子之責者所當知而
今日行之之序所自始焉者也〔臣〕草茅疎賤未嘗入侍
帷幄親奉
旒扆以仰窺所謂戒懼慎獨之功然讀憫災儆變之諭知
陛下有畏天命之心觀守成由舊之政知
陛下有畏
祖宗之心至於人材之進退奏䟽之可否又有以知
陛下有畏公議之心畏之一言戒懼慎獨之明驗也而〔臣〕
猶諄諄言之不置者誠以矜持於天下耳目所共及
者易為力存省於一己耳目所不及者難為功伏願
===
陛下於萬幾方暇之際一念未萌之時雖不必明堂聽政
也而正衣冠尊瞻視儼乎如百官之臨雖不必宣室
致齋也而定思慮絕嗜慾凛乎如上帝之對使本源
澄澈如明鏡止水照之而無不見使方寸軒豁如空
谷虛室納之而無不容及夫卒然之頃一念之萌又
必察其果出於天理之公而天下民物所同欲乎則
毅然行之惟恐其不力果出於人欲之私而天下民
物所共惡乎則斷然去之惟恐其不至愛憎之動則
察其所愛而欲近之與所憎而欲遠之者何人喜懼
之發則察其所喜而樂為與所懼而不敢為者何事

陛下於萬幾方暇之際一念未萌之蹟雖不必明堂聽政
也而正衣冠尊瞻視儼乎如百官之臨雖不必宣室
致齋也而定思慮絕嗜慾凜乎如上帝之對使本源

谷靈室納之而無不容夏夫卒然之頃一念之萌又
必察其果出於天理之公而天下民物所同欲乎則
毅然行之惟恐其不力果出於人欲之私而天下民
物所共惡乎則斷然去之惟恐其不至愛憎之動則
察其所愛而欲近之與所憎而欲遠之者何人喜懼
之發則察其所喜而樂為與所懼而不敢為者何事
punctuated:
之事也。此欲盡宗子之責者所當知，而今日行之之序所自始焉者也。

〔臣〕草茅疎賤，未嘗入侍帷幄，親奉旒扆，以仰窺所謂戒懼慎獨之功。然讀憫災儆變之諭，知陛下有畏天命之心；觀守成由舊之政，知陛下有畏祖宗之心；至於人材之進退、奏䟽之可否，又有以知陛下有畏公議之心。畏之一言，戒懼慎獨之明驗也。而〔臣〕猶諄諄言之不置者，誠以矜持於天下耳目所共及者易為力，存省於一己耳目所不及者難為功。

伏願陛下於萬幾方暇之際、一念未萌之時，雖不必明堂聽政也，而正衣冠，尊瞻視，儼乎如百官之臨；雖不必宣室致齋也，而定思慮，絕嗜慾，凛乎如上帝之對。使本源澄澈，如明鏡止水，照之而無不見；使方寸軒豁，如空谷虛室，納之而無不容。及夫卒然之頃、一念之萌，又必察其果出於天理之公，而天下民物所同欲乎，則毅然行之，惟恐其不力；果出於人欲之私，而天下民物所共惡乎，則斷然去之，惟恐其不至。愛憎之動，則察其所愛而欲近之與所憎而欲遠之者何人；喜懼之發，則察其所喜而樂為與所懼而不敢為者何事。
translation_en:
… is the practice of vigilance in solitude. This is what anyone wishing to fulfill the responsibility of the lineage heir must understand, and where the sequence of putting it into practice today must begin.

Your servant is an obscure and lowly man of the countryside. I have never attended within the imperial chambers or personally served before the throne, so as reverently to observe your efforts at watchfulness, apprehension, and vigilance in solitude. Yet, reading your edicts expressing compassion over disasters and warning against anomalous events, I know that Your Majesty holds Heaven’s Mandate in awe. Observing your policies of preserving inherited achievements and following established precedents, I know that Your Majesty holds the imperial ancestors in awe. From the advancement and dismissal of men of talent, and the approval or rejection of memorials, I further know that Your Majesty holds public judgment in awe. This single word, “awe,” is clear evidence of watchfulness, apprehension, and vigilance in solitude. That your servant nevertheless speaks of these earnestly and unceasingly is because maintaining a disciplined bearing where all the world can see and hear is easy, whereas preserving and examining the mind where even one’s own eyes and ears cannot reach is difficult.

I humbly beseech Your Majesty, in moments of respite from the myriad affairs of state, before a single thought has arisen: even when not hearing affairs of government in the Hall of Light, straighten your robes and cap and maintain a dignified gaze, as solemnly as though the hundred officials stood before you; even when not undertaking ritual purification in the Xuanshi Hall, settle your thoughts and cut off cravings, as reverently as though confronting the Lord on High. Make the original source of your mind limpid and clear, like a bright mirror or still water, reflecting everything without exception. Make your heart spacious and open, like an empty valley or unoccupied chamber, admitting everything and accommodating all. Then, when suddenly a single thought arises, you must examine it: does it truly issue from the impartiality of Heaven’s principle, and is it what the people and all beings under Heaven alike desire? If so, carry it out resolutely, fearing only that your effort may be insufficient. Does it issue from the selfishness of human desires, and is it what the people and all beings under Heaven alike abhor? If so, cast it away decisively, fearing only that you may not do so completely. When love or hatred stirs, examine who it is that you love and wish to draw near, and who it is that you hate and wish to keep at a distance; when delight or fear arises, examine what affairs delight you and make you willing to act, and what affairs frighten you and make you dare not act …

title: 弘治三年進士登科錄
text:
毋曰九重之邃一念之差人不得而知也天下之視
聽於是乎在焉毋曰五位之尊一事之失人不得而
非也神明之昭鑒於是乎存焉斯可謂之戒懼慎獨
而天之所以與我者為無慊矣由是推之以立制度
則制度之立此心也推之以行政令則政令之行此
心也推是心以養民自有以著保惠賙恤之實推是
心以教民自有以為轉移感動之機至於一法之廢
興則曰吾為天守法非吾所得而輕變也一錢之出
納則曰吾為天惜財非吾所得而妄費也一官之命
則曰此天之所以命有德者吾不得而專也一刑之
===
用則曰此天之所以討有罪者吾不得而私也凡吾
祖宗之所貽謀者期之於必行凡古帝王之所垂法者期
之於必可行斯可謂之善教善養而天之所以責我者
為無負矣如是而稱為天地之宗子真所謂踐形惟
肖者矣真所謂聖其合德者矣代天之功烏有不盡
配天之治烏有不成儒者之道烏有不極其至哉然
臣又聞之周公之告成王曰若生子罔不在厥初生

Preserve what has been achieved amid fullness and success, and remain vigilant after attaining ease and repose; persevere after the initial burst of effort, and gradually bring about enduring greatness. Then, in acting on Heaven’s behalf, you will accomplish unceasing self-strengthening; in matching Heaven, you will realize the subtle perfection of purity that likewise never ceases. title: 弘治三年進士登科錄
text:
臣劉存業
臣對臣聞上天生民全付斯道於一人人君代天全
體斯道於一身夫道之大原出於天具於人而所以
主張綱維之者則在乎君也苟渙然各付於品彙之
衆而不渾然全責之一人之身則散亂而無統汗漫
而無歸天地之大化育何自而成人物之衆生理何
自而遂此上天所以立君之意也人君膺代天之任
當斯道之責而不能彌綸造化統理人物天下之大
有一不遂其生而若其性則亦何以稱上天所付之
重哉然以一人之身任莫大之責將事事而爲之物
===
物而理之其爲力愈勤其爲心愈勞而其去道愈遠
矣此唐虞三代聖帝明王所以必加體道之功以全
其本然之天以極其功用之大若木之本大而末自
茂水之源深而流自長所操者約而所該者博所守
者近而所及者遠不出乎一身之間而成功與天地
民物相終始焉所謂易簡而天下之理得天下之理
得而成位乎其中者也後世若漢唐宋之君非無法
度之立政令之行而莫知所以反求諸身其於斯道
之責何如哉洪惟
皇帝陛下稟睿知之資撫休明之運奉天以敬恪勤父事

punctuated:
臣劉存業。
臣對：臣聞上天生民，全付斯道於一人；人君代天，全體斯道於一身。夫道之大原出於天，具於人，而所以主張綱維之者，則在乎君也。苟渙然各付於品彙之衆，而不渾然全責之一人之身，則散亂而無統，汗漫而無歸。天地之大，化育何自而成？人物之衆，生理何自而遂？此上天所以立君之意也。人君膺代天之任，當斯道之責，而不能彌綸造化，統理人物，天下之大，有一不遂其生而若其性，則亦何以稱上天所付之重哉？然以一人之身，任莫大之責，將事事而爲之，物物而理之，其爲力愈勤，其爲心愈勞，而其去道愈遠矣。此唐虞三代聖帝明王所以必加體道之功，以全其本然之天，以極其功用之大。若木之本大而末自茂，水之源深而流自長，所操者約而所該者博，所守者近而所及者遠，不出乎一身之間，而成功與天地民物相終始焉。所謂「易簡而天下之理得，天下之理得而成位乎其中」者也。後世若漢唐宋之君，非無法度之立、政令之行，而莫知所以反求諸身，其於斯道之責何如哉？洪惟皇帝陛下，稟睿知之資，撫休明之運，奉天以敬，恪勤父事
translation_en:
Your servant Liu Cunye.
Your servant replies: I have heard that Heaven above brings forth the people and entrusts this Way in its entirety to one person; the ruler acts on Heaven’s behalf and embodies this Way in its entirety in his own person. The great source of the Way issues from Heaven and is inherent in human beings, but it rests with the ruler to uphold it and maintain its ordering framework. If it were dispersed and separately entrusted to the multitude of beings, rather than responsibility for it being vested wholly in one person, it would be scattered without unity, diffuse without a point of return. Vast as Heaven and Earth are, how could their transforming and nourishing work be accomplished? Numerous as people and other beings are, how could the principles of their life find fulfillment? This is Heaven’s purpose in establishing a ruler. The ruler accepts the charge of acting on Heaven’s behalf and bears responsibility for this Way. If he cannot encompass the workings of creation and bring people and other beings under ordered governance—if, throughout the vast realm, even one fails to fulfill its life and follow its nature—how could he prove equal to the weighty trust Heaven has bestowed upon him? Yet if, bearing this immense responsibility in his single person, he seeks to undertake every affair and regulate every being individually, the more strenuous his exertions and the more wearied his mind, the farther he will depart from the Way.
This is why the sage emperors and enlightened kings of Tang, Yu, and the Three Dynasties invariably devoted themselves to embodying the Way, preserving intact their original, Heaven-given nature and fully realizing the greatness of its efficacy. Just as a tree with a stout root naturally has flourishing branches, and water with a deep source naturally flows far, what they grasped was concise, yet what it encompassed was broad; what they held to was near, yet its reach was distant. Without going beyond their own persons, their achievements endured from beginning to end with Heaven and Earth, the people, and all beings. This is what is meant by: “Through ease and simplicity, the principles of all under Heaven are grasped; once the principles of all under Heaven are grasped, one establishes one’s place in their midst.” As for the rulers of later ages, such as those of Han, Tang, and Song, it was not that they established no laws and institutions or implemented no administrative commands. Yet none understood how to turn back and seek within themselves. How, then, did they measure up to their responsibility for this Way?
I reverently reflect that Your Majesty the Emperor, endowed with sagely insight and presiding over an auspicious and enlightened age, serves Heaven with reverence, conscientiously and diligently attending to it as a father …

臣竊惟：「大哉乾元，萬物資始」，父之道也；「至哉坤元，萬物資生」，母之道也。人之有生，混然中處，天地之塞，吾其體；天地之帥，吾其性。性也者，道之全體也。然則有生之類，孰非天地之子，抑孰不具斯道於身乎？然天地之於其子，但能予之以道，而不能使之皆由之也。於是而立之大君焉。大君者，其衆子中之宗子歟？既曰天地之宗子，則豈徒貴之以九重之位，富之以四海之禄而已哉？盖必厚之以清明之資，重之以純粹之質，使之出乎其類，拔乎其萃，以為天地民物之主，而斯道之責全寄於一人之身矣。是故典曰天敘，而惇之者君；禮曰天秩，而庸之者君；賞曰天命，刑曰天討，而予

…the heart of one serving his father; you nurture all things with compassion, hoping to foster a custom in which the people come to you as children. Your blessings flow abundantly, and your virtue accords with the boundless virtue of Heaven. Throughout all lands beneath Heaven, everyone sings praises and leaps for joy. Today we behold once more the harmonious rule under which phoenixes appear and beasts dance. Now, in a respite from your myriad affairs, you have specially summoned us, your servants, to court and graciously bestowed your august questions upon us. First, you ask about the Way by which a ruler succeeds Heaven and Earth and presides over the people and all things. Next, you examine the causes of good and bad government under Tang and Yu, the Three Dynasties, and the Han, Tang, and Song. Finally, you investigate the sequence in which this Way should be put into practice. Yet I am foolish and shallow: how could I fathom your profound intentions? Nevertheless, though merely a commoner from the countryside, I have been permitted to join the ranks of the gentlemen addressed here and to offer words before your embroidered throne screen. How could I dare withhold my innermost thoughts rather than present whatever small insight my foolishness has yielded?

Your servant humbly reflects: “Great indeed is the originating power of Qian; all things depend upon it for their beginning”—this is the Way of the father. “Perfect indeed is the originating power of Kun; all things depend upon it for their birth”—this is the Way of the mother. Human beings, upon coming into existence, dwell amid Heaven and Earth as part of their undivided whole. What fills Heaven and Earth constitutes my body; what commands Heaven and Earth constitutes my nature. Nature is the Way in its entirety. Among all living beings, then, who is not a child of Heaven and Earth? And who does not possess this Way within themselves? Yet Heaven and Earth can only endow their children with the Way; they cannot make them all follow it. Thus a great ruler is established for them. Is not the great ruler the principal heir among their many children? Since he is called the principal heir of Heaven and Earth, could this mean merely ennobling him with the throne within the ninefold palace and enriching him with the revenues of all within the Four Seas? Surely he must be generously endowed with clarity and understanding, and richly furnished with a pure and unalloyed constitution, so that he rises above his kind and excels among his fellows, becoming lord over Heaven and Earth, the people, and all things. Responsibility for this Way is thus entrusted entirely to the person of the ruler alone. Hence the enduring norms are called Heaven’s ordering, but it is the ruler who strengthens them; ritual is called Heaven’s ranking, but it is the ruler who puts it into practice. 寄宗子之責不亦大乎為宗子者繼承父母君主天
下則視天下之民皆吾同胞一氣而凡疲癃殘疾惸
獨鰥寡皆吾兄弟之顛連無告者也痒疴疾痛何者
不切於吾身乎故必思養之有道以遂其生敎之有
方以復其性使天下為一家中國為一人然後斯道
之責無不盡而宗子之稱可以無愧也不然則求為
天地惟肖之子且不可得況曰天地之宗子以主張
綱維乎斯道也哉臣嘗質諸經訂諸史而考諸往古
矣大哉帝堯存心於天下加志於窮民君哉帝舜有
慘怛之愛有忠利之敎其養民也命稷播百穀而烝
民乃粒其敎民也命契敷五敎而五品克遜宗子之
責可謂盡矣故當時萬邦協和四方風動百世之下
稱至治者必歸焉至於三代養民之政夏后氏五十
而貢殷人七十而助周人百畝而徹制雖或異其取
之以什一則不異敎民之政夏之學曰東序西序殷
之學曰左學右學周之學曰東膠虞庠名雖不同其
所以明人倫則同宗子之責亦可謂盡矣故有夏之東

punctuated:
奪之者君。民生未遂，賴之以養也；民性未復，賴之以敎也。天地之所以範圍、萬物之所以曲成，悉於此乎寄。宗子之責，不亦大乎？為宗子者，繼承父母，君主天下，則視天下之民皆吾同胞一氣，而凡疲癃殘疾、惸獨鰥寡，皆吾兄弟之顛連無告者也。痒疴疾痛，何者不切於吾身乎？故必思養之有道，以遂其生；敎之有方，以復其性，使天下為一家，中國為一人。然後斯道之責無不盡，而宗子之稱可以無愧也。不然，則求為天地惟肖之子且不可得，況曰天地之宗子，以主張綱維乎斯道也哉？
臣嘗質諸經，訂諸史，而考諸往古矣。大哉帝堯，存心於天下，加志於窮民！君哉帝舜，有慘怛之愛，有忠利之敎！其養民也，命稷播百穀，而烝民乃粒；其敎民也，命契敷五敎，而五品克遜。宗子之責，可謂盡矣。故當時萬邦協和，四方風動，百世之下，稱至治者必歸焉。
至於三代養民之政，夏后氏五十而貢，殷人七十而助，周人百畝而徹，制雖或異，其取之以什一則不異。敎民之政，夏之學曰東序、西序，殷之學曰左學、右學，周之學曰東膠、虞庠，名雖不同，其所以明人倫則同。宗子之責，亦可謂盡矣。故有夏之東漸西被，有商之式于九圍，成周之四海永清，良有以
translation_en:
…and it is the ruler who takes them away. When the people's livelihood is not yet secured, they depend upon him for sustenance; when their moral nature has not yet been restored, they depend upon him for instruction. The ordering work of Heaven and Earth and the bringing of all things to fulfillment in their particular ways are entirely entrusted to him. Is not the responsibility of their principal heir great? As their principal heir, he succeeds his parents and rules all under Heaven. He therefore regards all the people under Heaven as his siblings, sharing the same vital breath; all who are infirm or disabled, orphaned or alone, widowers or widows, are his brothers and sisters in distress, with no one to whom they can appeal. Of their ailments and sufferings, which does he not feel keenly in his own person? Thus he must consider how to sustain them properly, so that their lives may reach fulfillment, and how to instruct them effectively, so that their moral nature may be restored. He must make all under Heaven one family and the Central Kingdom one person. Only then will his responsibility for this Way be fully discharged, and he may bear the title of principal heir without shame. Otherwise, he cannot even hope to be a son who truly resembles Heaven and Earth. How much less could he be called their principal heir, charged with upholding and maintaining this Way!
Your servant has examined this against the Classics, checked it against the histories, and investigated antiquity. Great indeed was Emperor Yao: he kept all under Heaven in his heart and gave particular attention to the destitute! Truly a ruler was Emperor Shun: his love was deeply compassionate, and his instruction devoted to the people's benefit! To sustain the people, he commanded Ji to sow the various grains, and the multitude thereby had grain to eat. To instruct the people, he commanded Xie to disseminate the five teachings, and the five human relationships were duly ordered. He may be said to have fully discharged the responsibility of the principal heir. Thus, in that age, the myriad states lived in harmony, and the four quarters responded as though moved by the wind. Even a hundred generations later, anyone speaking of consummate government inevitably turns to them.
As for the policies for sustaining the people under the Three Dynasties, the rulers of Xia allotted fifty mu and employed the tribute system; the people of Yin allotted seventy mu and employed the labor-assistance system; and the people of Zhou allotted a hundred mu and employed the che levy system. Although their institutions differed, they were alike in taking one-tenth. As for policies for instructing the people, the schools of Xia were called the Eastern and Western Xu; those of Yin, the Left and Right Schools; and those of Zhou, the Eastern Jiao and the Yu Xiang. Although their names differed, their purpose of clarifying human relationships was the same. They too may be said to have fully discharged the responsibility of the principal heir. Thus Xia's influence spread eastward and extended westward; Shang became a model for the nine regions; and under the established Zhou, all within the Four Seas enjoyed enduring peace. There was indeed reason for this…

title: 弘治三年進士登科錄
text:
也自時厥後漢有蠲租之詔有代田之制唐有口分
世業有租庸調法宋有經界之令有均田之議其見
於制度政令之間者亦不可謂無意於養民也漢有
登用文學之典有宗戚受學之義唐有弘文館大學
之類以處王屬貴胄有廣文館書學之類以處臣民
俊秀宋有大學宗學武學以分其流有外舍内舍上
舍以進其等其見於制度政令之間者亦不可謂無
意於教民也然其治效之著雖至於海内富庶路不
拾遺户口繁庶求如古之出作入息耕田鑿井而但
知順帝之則則未也雖至於黎民醇厚縱囚來歸道
===
學可稱求如古之人人君子比屋可封而不知帝力
之何有則未也是其於宗子之責猶不能無歉焉夫
自唐虞而下至於漢唐宋諸君均一乾父坤母而為
天之子也其制度之立政令之行均一代天而理物
也然其治效之不同如此何哉是非世道升降爾殊
也存乎其君體道之功何如耳且夫道也者原於天
命之性具於人心之微而散見於日用事為之際要
其極至可以位天地可以育萬物可以參天地可以
賛化育是吾儒之所謂道而非異端虚無寂滅之謂
也蓋嘗求諸吾心而驗之矣思慮未發一真自如道

punctuated:
也。自時厥後，漢有蠲租之詔，有代田之制；唐有口分、世業，有租庸調法；宋有經界之令，有均田之議。其見於制度政令之間者，亦不可謂無意於養民也。漢有登用文學之典，有宗戚受學之義；唐有弘文館、大學之類，以處王屬貴胄，有廣文館、書學之類，以處臣民俊秀；宋有大學、宗學、武學，以分其流，有外舍、内舍、上舍，以進其等。其見於制度政令之間者，亦不可謂無意於教民也。然其治效之著，雖至於海内富庶、路不拾遺、户口繁庶，求如古之出作入息、耕田鑿井，而但知順帝之則，則未也；雖至於黎民醇厚、縱囚來歸、道學可稱，求如古之人人君子、比屋可封，而不知帝力之何有，則未也。是其於宗子之責，猶不能無歉焉。
夫自唐虞而下，至於漢、唐、宋諸君，均一乾父坤母，而為天之子也；其制度之立、政令之行，均一代天而理物也。然其治效之不同如此，何哉？是非世道升降爾殊也，存乎其君體道之功何如耳。
且夫道也者，原於天命之性，具於人心之微，而散見於日用事為之際。要其極至，可以位天地，可以育萬物，可以參天地，可以賛化育。是吾儒之所謂道，而非異端虚無寂滅之謂也。蓋嘗求諸吾心而驗之矣。思慮未發，一真自如，道
translation_en:
… there was good reason for this. From that time onward, the Han issued edicts remitting agricultural taxes and instituted the alternating-field system; the Tang established land allotments for individual subsistence and hereditary tenure, together with the system of grain tax, labor service, and cloth levy; and the Song issued orders to survey field boundaries and discussed equalizing landholdings. These institutions and administrative measures cannot be said to show no concern for nourishing the people. The Han had provisions for appointing men learned in the classics and principles governing the education of imperial relatives. The Tang maintained institutions such as the Institute for the Advancement of Literature and the Imperial University to accommodate imperial kinsmen and sons of the nobility, and institutions such as the Institute for the Extension of Literary Arts and the School of Calligraphy to accommodate outstanding talents among officials and commoners. The Song maintained the Imperial University, the School for Imperial Clansmen, and the Military School to distinguish their educational streams, and the Outer, Inner, and Upper Halls to advance students through successive grades. These institutions and administrative measures likewise cannot be said to show no concern for educating the people. Yet, however conspicuous the results of their government—even when the realm was prosperous, no one picked up property lost on the road, and the population flourished—they did not attain the condition of antiquity, when people went out to work and returned to rest, tilled fields and dug wells, knowing only to follow the Sovereign’s ordinances. Even when the common people were sincere and generous, released prisoners returned voluntarily, and learning of the Way was worthy of praise, they did not attain the condition of antiquity, when everyone was a gentleman, every household was worthy of enfeoffment, and people knew nothing of what the emperor’s power had contributed. Thus they still fell short in fulfilling their responsibility as the lineage’s principal heir.
From the rulers of Tang and Yu down to the monarchs of the Han, Tang, and Song, all alike had Qian as father and Kun as mother and were sons of Heaven. In establishing institutions and implementing administrative measures, all alike acted on Heaven’s behalf to bring order to all things. Why, then, did the results of their government differ so greatly? This was not simply a difference arising from the rise and decline of the times. It depended on how well their rulers worked to embody the Way.
The Way originates in the nature conferred by Heaven’s mandate, is fully present in the subtle recesses of the human mind, and manifests itself throughout the affairs and activities of daily life. At its utmost, it enables Heaven and Earth to take their proper places, the myriad things to be nourished, and human beings to form a triad with Heaven and Earth and assist their transforming and nourishing work. This is what we Confucians call the Way; it is not the emptiness, nothingness, quiescence, and extinction spoken of by heterodox teachings. I have sought it within my own mind and verified it there. Before thought and deliberation arise, the single, genuine reality remains naturally itself—the Way’s …

title: 弘治三年進士登科錄
text:
之體也虛靈知覺感而遂通道之用也惟其存於中
者常肅然而不亂炯然而不昏則靜而道之體無不
全動而道之用無不行矣若夫不能不囿於氣而又
不能不動於欲則將為氣所昏為欲所蔽而道之體
用亦隨之而昏且亂焉是雖一身一家且將無如之
何烏有所謂位育參贊之功哉古之人君惟唐堯虞
舜生而知之安而行之故能全體是道而無愧觀其
執中精一之傳槩可見矣若夫夏禹商湯周武其聰
明之質固已不能如堯舜之至惟能學而知之利而
行之故亦有以復其德性聰明之本然而體是道之
===
全以造乎堯舜之域觀禹之安止湯之建中武之建
極亦可見矣孔子所謂及其成功一也漢唐宋以下
非無願治之主而莫克有志於斯是以隨時遷就而
終不得以與夫帝王之盛其或耻為庸主而思用力
於此道又不免蔽於老子浮屠之說靜則以虛無寂
滅為樂而不知有所謂實理之原動則以應緣無礙
為達而不知有所謂善惡之幾若漢之文帝唐之太
宗宋之仁宗亦可謂一代之賢君也而皆不免乎此
賢者如此他可知矣是以日用之間內外乖離不相
為用區區制度政令之末亦何益於治哉

punctuated:
之體也。虛靈知覺，感而遂通，道之用也。惟其存於中者常肅然而不亂，炯然而不昏，則靜而道之體無不全，動而道之用無不行矣。若夫不能不囿於氣，而又不能不動於欲，則將為氣所昏，為欲所蔽，而道之體用亦隨之而昏且亂焉。是雖一身一家，且將無如之何，烏有所謂位育參贊之功哉？古之人君，惟唐堯虞舜生而知之，安而行之，故能全體是道而無愧。觀其執中精一之傳，槩可見矣。若夫夏禹商湯周武，其聰明之質固已不能如堯舜之至，惟能學而知之，利而行之，故亦有以復其德性聰明之本然，而體是道之全，以造乎堯舜之域。觀禹之安止、湯之建中、武之建極，亦可見矣。孔子所謂「及其成功，一也」。
漢唐宋以下，非無願治之主，而莫克有志於斯，是以隨時遷就，而終不得以與夫帝王之盛。其或耻為庸主，而思用力於此道，又不免蔽於老子浮屠之說。靜則以虛無寂滅為樂，而不知有所謂實理之原；動則以應緣無礙為達，而不知有所謂善惡之幾。若漢之文帝、唐之太宗、宋之仁宗，亦可謂一代之賢君也，而皆不免乎此。賢者如此，他可知矣。是以日用之間，內外乖離，不相為用，區區制度政令之末，亦何益於治哉？
translation_en:
…is the substance of the Way. The mind’s empty, numinous awareness, responding to stimuli and thereby comprehending them, is the functioning of the Way. If what abides within remains ever reverent and undisturbed, luminous and unobscured, then in stillness the substance of the Way will be wholly intact, and in activity its functioning will be fully realized. But if one cannot escape confinement by one’s vital endowment (qi), and cannot avoid being stirred by desires, then that endowment will cloud one and those desires will obscure one; the substance and functioning of the Way will accordingly become obscured and disordered. One will then be unable to manage even oneself and one’s household. How could one accomplish what is called setting Heaven and Earth in their proper places, nurturing the myriad things, forming a triad with Heaven and Earth, and assisting their transforming and nourishing work? Among ancient rulers, only Yao of Tang and Shun of Yu knew this from birth and practiced it with natural ease; thus they could embody this Way completely and without deficiency. This can broadly be seen in their transmission of the teachings on holding fast to the Mean and being discerning and single-minded. As for Yu of Xia, Tang of Shang, and Wu of Zhou, their innate intelligence and discernment admittedly did not attain the perfection of Yao and Shun. Yet they could come to know it through study and practice it from recognition of its benefit. Thus they too could restore their moral nature and discernment to their original condition, embody this Way in its entirety, and attain the realm of Yao and Shun. This can also be seen in Yu’s resting in his proper place, Tang’s establishing the Mean, and Wu’s establishing the supreme standard. As Confucius said, “When they achieve success, they are alike.”
From the Han, Tang, and Song onward, there were certainly rulers who desired good government, but none could set their resolve upon this. Thus they accommodated themselves to circumstances and ultimately could not match the flourishing rule of the ancient emperors and kings. Those who were ashamed to be mediocre rulers and sought to devote their efforts to this Way nevertheless could not escape being misled by the teachings of Laozi and the Buddha. In stillness, they delighted in emptiness and extinction, unaware of what is called the source of substantive principle; in activity, they regarded responding to conditions without obstruction as mastery, unaware of what are called the incipient distinctions between good and evil. Emperor Wen of Han, Taizong of Tang, and Renzong of Song may each be called a worthy ruler of his age, yet none escaped this failing. If even the worthy were like this, the others may readily be judged. Thus, in their daily conduct, the inner and outer were at odds and failed to support each other. What benefit to government could there be in the mere outward details of institutions, administrative orders, and decrees?

title: 弘治三年進士登科錄
text:
陛下聰明而仁恕剛毅而中正口代天言心代天意手代
天工身代天事於帝王致治之道上天付托之重固
已身體而力行之矣

得其行之之序臣恭仰
聖德巍巍蕩蕩不可以有加矣夫復何言竊意聖人之

punctuated: 陛下聰明而仁恕，剛毅而中正，口代天言，心代天意，手代天工，身代天事。於帝王致治之道、上天付托之重，固已身體而力行之矣。制策惓惓，思盡宗子之責，比隆古之聖帝明王，而又欲得其行之之序。臣恭仰聖德巍巍蕩蕩，不可以有加矣，夫復何言？竊意聖人之心無窮，道已至矣，而猶以為未至。此臣所以望於陛下者，亦有加而無已也。所謂行之之序，無他，亦培養其本原而已矣。夫道之體用，本然全具。人惟靜而不知所以養之，則大本有所不立，而無以為酬酢萬變之主；動而不知所以察之，則達道有所不行，而無以為應事接物之用。臣伏願陛下自不覩不聞之前，而致其戒慎恐懼者愈嚴愈敬，以至無一毫之偏倚，而守之常不失焉；尤於隱微幽獨之際，而謹其善惡之幾者愈精愈密，以至無一毫之差繆，而行之每不違焉。夫至靜之中無所偏倚，則有以致其中，而大本以立；應物之處無少乖戾，則有以致其和，而達道以行。有中以為之本，則存於心者無妄思；有和以為之用，則施之事者無妄動。以之養民也，莫非精神心術之寓；以之教民也，莫非躬行心得
translation_en:
Your Majesty is discerning, humane, and forgiving; resolute, balanced, and upright. Your mouth speaks for Heaven, your mind expresses Heaven’s intent, your hands perform Heaven’s work, and your person carries out Heaven’s affairs. You have indeed embodied and vigorously put into practice the Way by which emperors and kings achieve good government, bearing the weighty trust Heaven has placed in you. Your policy question earnestly expresses your desire to fulfill your responsibility as Heaven’s principal son, to match the greatness of the sage emperors and enlightened kings of antiquity, and also to learn the proper sequence for putting this into practice. Your servant reverently looks up to your lofty and boundless sagely virtue, to which nothing could be added. What more, then, can I say? Yet I humbly think that the sage’s mind knows no bounds: even when he has attained the Way, he still regards himself as not yet having attained it. Thus what your servant hopes for from Your Majesty likewise continues to increase without end. The proper sequence of practice consists simply in nurturing its fundamental source.

The substance and functioning of the Way are inherently present in their entirety. But if a person in stillness does not know how to nurture them, the great foundation will not be fully established, and there will be no governing center for responding to countless changes. If, when active, he does not know how to examine them, the universally applicable Way will not be fully practiced, and there will be no means of responding to affairs and engaging with things. Your servant humbly wishes that Your Majesty, even before anything is seen or heard, will exercise vigilance and apprehension with ever greater rigor and reverence, until there is not the slightest leaning or bias, and will hold to this constantly without losing it. Especially amid what is hidden and subtle, in solitude, may you attend to the first stirrings of good and evil with ever greater precision and care, until there is not the slightest error, and never depart from this in your conduct.

For when there is no leaning or bias amid utter stillness, equilibrium can be fully realized and the great foundation established. When there is not the slightest discord in responding to things, harmony can be fully realized and the universally applicable Way put into practice. With equilibrium as the foundation, the mind harbors no errant thoughts; with harmony as its functioning, action in affairs involves no errant moves. Applied to nourishing the people, all of this gives expression to your spirit and the workings of your mind; applied to teaching the people, all of it flows from what you practice personally and apprehend in your heart…

title: 弘治三年進士登科錄
text:
之餘推之於中國則中國為一人推之於天下則天
下為一家無一夫不遂其飽食暖衣之願無一人不
入於漸仁摩義之區由是陰陽動靜各止其所而天
地於此乎位充塞無間驩欣交通而萬物於此乎育
是則天位乎上地位乎下聖人成位乎中而可以與
天地並立為三矣易曰后以財成天地之道輔相天
地之宜以左右民書曰惟其克相上帝禮曰天子者
與天地參此之謂也此萬化之本原一心之妙用聖
神之能事學問之極功臣前所謂所操者約而所該
者博所守者近而所及者遠上天立君之意畢於此
===
人君繼天之事盡於此矣
陛下宜留意焉臣又聞之易曰天行健君子以自强不息
陛下日御經筵講求至理紬繹六經之文探索儒先之蘊
於戒懼慎獨之說固已習聞之矣然進銳退速亦人
情之常而古先聖王之所深戒者也設若敬畏未幾
而慢忽繼之檢束未幾而侈泰隨之勤惰之靡常暴
寒之不一則豈所謂自彊不息之誠而何以極體道
之功哉伊尹告太甲曰嗣王祗厥身念哉周公告成
王曰嚴恭寅畏天命自度召公之誥曰嗚呼柰何弗
敬伊周召公皆古之聖賢而所以啓迪其君欲其無

punctuated:
之餘。推之於中國，則中國為一人；推之於天下，則天下為一家。無一夫不遂其飽食暖衣之願，無一人不入於漸仁摩義之區。由是陰陽動靜，各止其所，而天地於此乎位；充塞無間，驩欣交通，而萬物於此乎育。是則天位乎上，地位乎下，聖人成位乎中，而可以與天地並立為三矣。《易》曰：「后以財成天地之道，輔相天地之宜，以左右民。」《書》曰：「惟其克相上帝。」《禮》曰：「天子者，與天地參。」此之謂也。此萬化之本原，一心之妙用，聖神之能事，學問之極功。臣前所謂所操者約而所該者博，所守者近而所及者遠，上天立君之意畢於此，人君繼天之事盡於此矣。陛下宜留意焉。
臣又聞之，《易》曰：「天行健，君子以自强不息。」陛下日御經筵，講求至理，紬繹六經之文，探索儒先之蘊，於戒懼慎獨之說，固已習聞之矣。然進銳退速，亦人情之常，而古先聖王之所深戒者也。設若敬畏未幾而慢忽繼之，檢束未幾而侈泰隨之，勤惰之靡常，暴寒之不一，則豈所謂自彊不息之誠，而何以極體道之功哉？伊尹告太甲曰：「嗣王祗厥身，念哉！」周公告成王曰：「嚴恭寅畏，天命自度。」召公之誥曰：「嗚呼！柰何弗敬？」伊、周、召公皆古之聖賢，而所以啓迪其君，欲其無
translation_en:
…the overflow of personal practice and understanding gained in the heart. Extend this to the Central Kingdom, and the Central Kingdom becomes one person; extend it to all under Heaven, and all under Heaven becomes one family. Not a single man will fail to fulfill his wish for sufficient food and warm clothing; not a single person will remain outside the realm of immersion in benevolence and cultivation through righteousness. Thus yin and yang, activity and stillness, each rest in their proper place, and Heaven and Earth are thereby rightly situated. All is filled without a gap, with joyful communication throughout, and the myriad things are thereby nourished. Heaven then occupies its place above, Earth its place below, and the sage takes his place between them, able to stand alongside Heaven and Earth as one of the Three Powers. The Book of Changes says: “The ruler shapes and completes the Way of Heaven and Earth, assists what is fitting to Heaven and Earth, and thereby guides the people.” The Book of Documents says: “He alone can assist the Lord on High.” The Book of Rites says: “The Son of Heaven forms a triad with Heaven and Earth.” This is what these passages mean. This is the source of all transformations, the wondrous functioning of the single mind, the achievement of sagely and spiritual wisdom, and the highest accomplishment of learning. It is what your servant referred to earlier: what one holds to is simple, yet what it encompasses is broad; what one preserves is close at hand, yet its reach is distant. Heaven’s purpose in establishing a ruler is fulfilled here, and the ruler’s work of carrying on Heaven’s task is fully realized here. Your Majesty should give this your attention.
Your servant has also heard these words from the Book of Changes: “Heaven’s movement is vigorous; the gentleman accordingly strengthens himself without ceasing.” Your Majesty attends the Classics Colloquium daily, investigating ultimate principles, drawing out the meaning of the Six Classics, and exploring the depths of earlier Confucian scholars’ thought. You have certainly heard often the teachings on vigilance, apprehension, and watchfulness over oneself when alone. Yet advancing eagerly and retreating swiftly is also a common human tendency, and one against which the sage kings of antiquity warned most earnestly. Suppose that reverent awe is soon followed by negligence, and self-restraint soon gives way to extravagance and indulgence; if diligence and idleness alternate unpredictably, like exposure now to warmth and now to cold, how could this be the sincerity meant by strengthening oneself without ceasing? And how could one thereby bring the work of embodying the Way to its fullest accomplishment? Yi Yin told Tai Jia: “Let the successor king be reverent in his person. Be mindful!” The Duke of Zhou told King Cheng: “Be solemnly respectful and reverently fearful; measure yourself against Heaven’s mandate.” The Duke of Shao’s admonition says: “Alas! How can one fail to be reverent?” Yi Yin, the Duke of Zhou, and the Duke of Shao were all sages and worthies of antiquity. In instructing and guiding their rulers, they wished them never…

title: 弘治三年進士登科錄
text:
時無處而不用力於戒慎者如出一口此臣所以懇
懇為終篇獻也伏願
陛下法剛健之德致不息之誠一日二日而此心之戒慎
不以一日二日而殊微言細行而此心之戒慎不以
微言細行而異若堯之兢兢若舜之業業若禹之克
勤若湯之日新若武之肅將若元氣之運行而四時
之流通則始終此心始終此治矣伏惟
陛下留神採納則天下幸甚臣干瀆
天威不勝戰慄臣謹對

懇爲終篇獻也伏願

天威不勝戰慄〔臣〕謹對
punctuated: 時無處而不用力於戒慎者，如出一口。此臣所以懇懇為終篇獻也。伏願陛下法剛健之德，致不息之誠，一日二日，而此心之戒慎不以一日二日而殊；微言細行，而此心之戒慎不以微言細行而異。若堯之兢兢，若舜之業業，若禹之克勤，若湯之日新，若武之肅將，若元氣之運行而四時之流通，則始終此心，始終此治矣。伏惟陛下留神採納，則天下幸甚。臣干瀆天威，不勝戰慄。臣謹對。
translation_en: …at every time and in every place to exert himself in vigilance and caution: they spoke as though with one voice. This is why your servant earnestly offers this counsel at the close of his essay. I humbly wish that Your Majesty would emulate the virtue of strength and vigor and attain unceasing sincerity. From one day to the next, let the vigilance and caution of this mind remain unchanged with the passing days; in the smallest words and deeds, let that vigilance and caution remain undiminished by their triviality. Be wary as Yao was, watchful as Shun was, diligent as Yu was, daily renewed as Tang was, and reverent in carrying out your duties as King Wu was. Be like the movement of the primordial vital force and the circulation of the four seasons. Then this disposition of mind will endure from beginning to end, and so will this good governance. If Your Majesty would graciously give this counsel your attention and adopt it, all under Heaven would be most fortunate. Your servant has presumptuously affronted the imperial majesty and trembles beyond measure. Your servant respectfully submits this reply.

title: 弘治三年進士登科錄

punctuated:
臣靳貴。
臣對：臣聞人君受天地之命，以盡安民之責，惟在於體仁而已矣。盖仁者，天地生物之心，而人所得以生者也。貫四德，統萬善，至大而無外，至公而無私，至正而不頗者也。人君能體乎仁，則天理周流，物我無間，以萬物為一體，視中國猶一人，視天下猶一家，而所以盡安民之責者，豈外乎是哉？是以養民而各遂其生，教民而各復其性，天地自此而位，萬物自此而育。凡天地責於我者，舉無所負，而可以與天地參矣，豈不克盡宗子之責也哉？然惟古昔帝王能與於此，而漢唐宋之君所不能逮焉者也。
欽惟皇帝陛下，憲天聰明，法天剛健，日新又新之德，一天行之不息；無偏無黨之化，一天覆之無私。曩在青宫，天命已凝於主鬯；比登紫極，天道大布於寰區。蠲租稅，罷貢獻，萬民莫不涵泳者，猶天之雨露；抑僥倖，斥異端，萬邦莫不鼓舞者，猶天之雷霆。誠德肖天地而首出庶物者也。茲猶廷集多士，俯賜綸音，首引《西銘》之言，謂人君為天地宗子，其責至大，
translation_en:
Your servant, Jin Gui.
Your servant replies: I have heard that the ruler receives the mandate of Heaven and Earth to fulfill his responsibility to bring peace to the people, and that this lies solely in embodying benevolence. Benevolence is the life-giving heart of Heaven and Earth, which human beings receive in order to live. It runs through the four virtues and unites all goodness; it is supremely great, leaving nothing outside it, supremely impartial, without selfishness, and supremely upright, without deviation. If the ruler can embody benevolence, heavenly principle circulates everywhere, with no separation between self and other. He regards the myriad things as one body, the central realm as one person, and all under Heaven as one family. Could the means of fulfilling his responsibility to bring peace to the people lie outside this? Thus he nourishes the people so that each may fulfill the course of life, and teaches them so that each may recover their inherent nature. Through this, Heaven and Earth take their proper places and the myriad things are nurtured. He fails in none of the responsibilities that Heaven and Earth impose upon him, and can stand alongside them as a third. Is this not fully discharging the responsibility of their principal heir? Yet only the emperors and kings of antiquity could attain this; the rulers of the Han, Tang, and Song could not reach it.
I reverently consider that Your Majesty the Emperor models your intelligence upon Heaven and takes Heaven’s strength and vigor as your pattern. Your virtue, renewed daily and renewed yet again, accords with Heaven’s ceaseless movement; your transforming influence, without bias or faction, accords with Heaven’s impartial sheltering of all. Formerly, when you dwelt in the crown prince’s palace, Heaven’s mandate had already become firmly vested in you as the one who would preside over the sacrificial wine. When you ascended the imperial throne, Heaven’s Way spread widely throughout the realm. You remitted taxes and abolished tribute offerings, and all the people were steeped in your bounty, as in Heaven’s rain and dew. You curbed those seeking unmerited favor and rejected heterodox teachings, and all the lands were stirred and heartened, as by Heaven’s thunder. Truly, your virtue resembles Heaven and Earth, and you stand foremost among the myriad beings. Even now, you have assembled the many scholars at court and graciously bestowed your imperial words. You began by citing the Western Inscription (Xi ming), stating that the ruler is the principal heir of Heaven and Earth and that his responsibility is supremely great …

text:
次舉歷代帝王之事以考其得失之原末復欲聞行
之之序自何而始臣伏而讀之又有以見
陛下於仁道之大信能真知而無疑矣尊其所聞行其所
知則比隆古之聖帝明王以無愧於宗子之責者特
易易耳臣復何言雖然受言之君不世出得言之時
不易逢臣幸際得言之時而遇受言之
君安得不罄其愚直以對揚
休命乎臣竊惟天地之於萬物雖高下異體然同此一
理同此一氣耳萬物則天地之所付與天地則萬物
之所自出故天地之於萬物有父母之義焉然萬物
===
均為天地之子而大君獨為宗子者則以天地生物
厚於人而尤厚於大君其縱之以德也曰天德其寵
之以位也曰天位其厚之以玉食之養也曰天禄其
寄之以政教之事也曰天職盖雖同生乎萬物之中
而實特出乎萬物之表乃托之繼承天地統理民物
者故張載論乾父坤母而以大君歸之宗子焉夫宗
子云者父母之嫡嗣衆子之所宗也一家之中痒痾
疾痛何者不切於身喜怒舒慘何者不關於意視其
飢寒則惕然思所以衣食之視其昏愚則惻然思所
以教育之凡可以周其生導其善者惟恐弗至必其

次舉歷代帝王之事，以考其得失之原，末復欲聞行之之序，自何而始。臣伏而讀之，又有以見陛下於仁道之大，信能真知而無疑矣。尊其所聞，行其所知，則比隆古之聖帝明王，以無愧於宗子之責者，特易易耳。臣復何言？雖然，受言之君不世出，得言之時不易逢。臣幸際得言之時，而遇受言之君，安得不罄其愚直，以對揚休命乎？
臣竊惟天地之於萬物，雖高下異體，然同此一理，同此一氣耳。萬物則天地之所付與，天地則萬物之所自出，故天地之於萬物，有父母之義焉。然萬物均為天地之子，而大君獨為宗子者，則以天地生物，厚於人，而尤厚於大君。其縱之以德也曰天德，其寵之以位也曰天位，其厚之以玉食之養也曰天禄，其寄之以政教之事也曰天職。盖雖同生乎萬物之中，而實特出乎萬物之表，乃托之繼承天地、統理民物者。故張載論乾父坤母，而以大君歸之宗子焉。
夫宗子云者，父母之嫡嗣，衆子之所宗也。一家之中，痒痾疾痛，何者不切於身？喜怒舒慘，何者不關於意？視其飢寒，則惕然思所以衣食之；視其昏愚，則惻然思所以教育之。凡可以周其生、導其善者，惟恐弗至，必其
translation_en:
…Next, you cited the deeds of emperors and kings of successive ages to examine the sources of their successes and failures. Finally, you wished to hear about the order in which to put this into practice: where should one begin? Your servant has reverently read these words and sees further evidence that Your Majesty truly understands, without doubt, the greatness of the Way of benevolence. By honoring what you have heard and practicing what you know, you can readily equal the grandeur of the sage emperors and enlightened kings of antiquity and fulfill without shame the responsibilities of the principal heir. What more could your servant say? Nevertheless, a ruler receptive to counsel does not appear in every age, and an opportunity to speak is not easily encountered. Your servant is fortunate to have such an opportunity and to meet a ruler willing to listen. How could I fail to offer all my simple candor in grateful response to your gracious command?
Your servant humbly considers that, although Heaven and Earth and the myriad things differ in elevation and form, they share this one principle and this one vital force. The myriad things receive their endowment from Heaven and Earth, and Heaven and Earth are the source from which the myriad things emerge. Thus Heaven and Earth stand as parents to the myriad things. Yet although all the myriad things are equally children of Heaven and Earth, the sovereign alone is their principal heir. This is because, in bringing things into being, Heaven and Earth are generous to human beings and especially generous to the sovereign. The virtue with which they endow him [?] is called heavenly virtue; the position with which they favor him is called the heavenly position; the sumptuous nourishment with which they enrich him is called heavenly emolument; and the affairs of government and instruction with which they entrust him are called heavenly duties. Although born among the myriad things, he truly stands above them: he is entrusted with succeeding Heaven and Earth and governing the people and all things. Thus, when Zhang Zai spoke of Qian as father and Kun as mother, he assigned the sovereign the role of principal heir.
The principal heir is the parents’ legitimate successor, the one whom all their other children acknowledge as head. Within a single family, whose ailments and pains does he not feel in his own body? Whose joy, anger, ease, or misery does he not take to heart? Seeing their hunger and cold, he anxiously considers how to clothe and feed them; seeing their ignorance and dullness, he compassionately considers how to educate and nurture them. In everything that might provide for their livelihood and guide them toward goodness, his sole fear is that his efforts may fall short. He must…

title: 弘治三年進士登科錄
text:
盡安衆子而後可以塞其責也大君之責何以異此
故必養之有道使凡身天地之氣以成形者無一不
安其生教之有方使凡心天地之理以為性者無一
不歸於善而宗子之責斯無負矣然此豈徒恃制度
政教者所能及哉臣故曰受天地之命以盡安民之
責惟在於體仁而已盖臣之所謂仁者非煦煦姑息
之謂也天下之正理本心之全德也在書則謂之中
易則謂之性與天道大學則謂之明德中庸則謂之
天命之性孟子則謂之仁義之心不特宗子有之而
凡為天地之子者無不有之也臣所謂體仁者亦非
===
比而效之之謂也仁為我之性情我為仁之楨榦也
即書之允執厥中易之盡性以至於命大學之克明
明德中庸之致中和孟子之充其仁義之心凡為天
地之子者皆所當然而大君任宗子之責則尤不容
以不然者也請以歷代之君證之古者洪水為灾民
生未遂也堯舜獨以為憂命禹以平水土命稷以教
稼穡不底於萬國咸寧不已焉逸居無教民性未復
也堯舜又以為憂命契以為司徒命夔以教胄子不
底於比屋可封不已焉其教養乎民者如此若乃三
代之制夏五十而貢殷七十而助及周而其法加詳

punctuated:
盡安衆子，而後可以塞其責也。大君之責何以異此？故必養之有道，使凡身天地之氣以成形者，無一不安其生；教之有方，使凡心天地之理以為性者，無一不歸於善，而宗子之責斯無負矣。然此豈徒恃制度政教者所能及哉？臣故曰：「受天地之命，以盡安民之責，惟在於體仁而已。」盖臣之所謂仁者，非煦煦姑息之謂也，天下之正理、本心之全德也。在《書》則謂之中，《易》則謂之性與天道，《大學》則謂之明德，《中庸》則謂之天命之性，《孟子》則謂之仁義之心。不特宗子有之，而凡為天地之子者，無不有之也。臣所謂體仁者，亦非比而效之之謂也。仁為我之性情，我為仁之楨榦也。即《書》之允執厥中，《易》之盡性以至於命，《大學》之克明明德，《中庸》之致中和，《孟子》之充其仁義之心。凡為天地之子者，皆所當然，而大君任宗子之責，則尤不容以不然者也。
請以歷代之君證之。古者洪水為灾，民生未遂也，堯舜獨以為憂，命禹以平水土，命稷以教稼穡，不底於萬國咸寧不已焉。逸居無教，民性未復也，堯舜又以為憂，命契以為司徒，命夔以教胄子，不底於比屋可封不已焉。其教養乎民者如此。若乃三代之制，夏五十而貢，殷七十而助，及周而其法加詳。
translation_en:
…bring well-being to all the sons, and only then can he fulfill his responsibility. How does the responsibility of the sovereign differ from this? He must therefore provide for them in the proper way, so that all who embody the vital energy of Heaven and Earth and thereby take form may live securely; and instruct them by appropriate means, so that all who take the principles of Heaven and Earth into their hearts as their nature may return to goodness. Only then will he have discharged the responsibility of the lineage’s principal heir. Yet how could this be achieved merely by relying on institutions, government, and instruction? Your servant therefore says: “To receive the mandate of Heaven and Earth and fulfill the responsibility of bringing well-being to the people depends solely on embodying benevolence.” By benevolence, your servant does not mean indulgent kindness, but the correct principles of all under Heaven and the complete virtue of the original heart. The Book of Documents calls it the Mean; the Book of Changes, human nature and the Way of Heaven; the Great Learning, luminous virtue; the Doctrine of the Mean, the nature conferred by Heaven’s mandate; and the Mencius, the heart of benevolence and righteousness. It is possessed not only by the principal heir: all who are children of Heaven and Earth possess it. Nor does your servant mean by embodying benevolence merely likening oneself to it and imitating it. Benevolence constitutes my nature and feelings; I am the supporting frame through which benevolence is realized. This is what the Book of Documents means by sincerely holding fast to the Mean; the Book of Changes, by fully realizing one’s nature and thereby attaining one’s destiny; the Great Learning, by being able to make luminous virtue shine forth; the Doctrine of the Mean, by bringing equilibrium and harmony to their fullest realization; and the Mencius, by fully developing the heart of benevolence and righteousness. All who are children of Heaven and Earth ought to do this; and the sovereign, bearing the responsibility of the principal heir, is especially bound to do so.
Allow me to substantiate this with the rulers of successive ages. In antiquity, great floods brought disaster, and the people could not secure their livelihoods. Yao and Shun took this especially to heart. They commanded Yu to regulate the waters and land, and Ji to teach sowing and reaping, never resting until all the myriad states were at peace. When the people lived at ease without instruction and their nature had not yet been restored, Yao and Shun again took this to heart. They appointed Xie as Minister of Education and commanded Kui to instruct the sons of the nobility, never resting until every household had people worthy of receiving a fief. Such was their care for the people’s instruction and sustenance. As for the institutions of the Three Dynasties, the Xia allotted fifty mu of land and employed the tribute system; the Yin allotted seventy mu and employed the labor-assistance system. Under the Zhou, these arrangements became more detailed…

title: 弘治三年進士登科錄
text:
鄉遂用貢法十夫有溝都鄙用助法八家同井耕則
通力而作收則計畝而分則當時固無無田之民亦
無過取之政也夏之學曰東序西序殷之學曰左學
右學及周而其法寢備家有塾黨有庠術有序國有
學八歲入小學十五入大學則當時固無不學之人
亦無無學之地也其教養乎民者又如此則唐虞三
代之時無一民不得其所矣豈非能盡宗子之責者
哉自是而後若漢之七制唐之三宗宋之真宗仁宗
皆表表可稱者然考其制度之立政令之行或二十
而稅一或減租以勸農或口分世業而節費以裕民
===
或遣官度田而課民以種植雖未嘗無意於養也然
井田不復而民之兼并自如經界不正而國之賦斂
無藝則所以養民者豈能使民生之盡遂乎或尊師
重傅而臨雍拜老或大召名儒而增廣生員或六學
之有領或三舍之有生雖未嘗無意於教也然躬行
未至而學校之設不周文辭是尚而教育之方未至
則所以教民者豈能使民性之盡復乎漢唐宋教養
乎民者僅能如此欲無一民之不得其所難矣其於
宗子之責能無負哉夫唐虞三代與夫漢唐宋之君
同此宗子之責同此制度政令之施而治效若是其

punctuated:
鄉遂用貢法，十夫有溝；都鄙用助法，八家同井。耕則通力而作，收則計畝而分，則當時固無無田之民，亦無過取之政也。夏之學曰東序、西序，殷之學曰左學、右學，及周而其法寢備，家有塾，黨有庠，術有序，國有學，八歲入小學，十五入大學，則當時固無不學之人，亦無無學之地也。其教養乎民者又如此，則唐虞三代之時，無一民不得其所矣。豈非能盡宗子之責者哉？
自是而後，若漢之七制、唐之三宗、宋之真宗、仁宗，皆表表可稱者。然考其制度之立、政令之行，或二十而稅一，或減租以勸農，或口分世業而節費以裕民，或遣官度田而課民以種植，雖未嘗無意於養也，然井田不復而民之兼并自如，經界不正而國之賦斂無藝，則所以養民者，豈能使民生之盡遂乎？或尊師重傅而臨雍拜老，或大召名儒而增廣生員，或六學之有領，或三舍之有生，雖未嘗無意於教也，然躬行未至而學校之設不周，文辭是尚而教育之方未至，則所以教民者，豈能使民性之盡復乎？漢唐宋教養乎民者僅能如此，欲無一民之不得其所，難矣。其於宗子之責，能無負哉？夫唐虞三代與夫漢唐宋之君，同此宗子之責，同此制度政令之施，而治效若是其
translation_en:
…In the townships and outlying districts, the tribute system was used, with a ditch for every ten cultivators’ holdings; in the landed domains, the labor-assistance system was used, with eight households sharing one well-field unit. In cultivation they pooled their labor, and at harvest they divided the yield according to acreage. Thus, in those days there were certainly no people without land and no government that exacted too much. The schools of the Xia were called the Eastern and Western Schools; those of the Yin, the Left and Right Schools. By the Zhou, the arrangements had gradually become complete: residential groups had local schools, neighborhood units had district schools, territorial units [?] had regional schools, and the capital had its schools. Children entered elementary learning at eight and advanced learning at fifteen. Thus, in those days there were certainly no people without schooling and no places without schools. Such, too, were their provisions for educating and sustaining the people. In the age of Tang and Yu and the Three Dynasties, therefore, not a single person failed to find a proper place. Were these not rulers who fully discharged the responsibility of the principal heir of the lineage?
Thereafter, such rulers as the seven sovereigns of the Han, the three Zong emperors of the Tang, and Zhenzong and Renzong of the Song were all outstanding and worthy of praise. Yet if we examine the institutions they established and the governmental commands they carried out, some levied a tax of one part in twenty; some reduced land taxes to encourage agriculture; some allotted land in personal and hereditary holdings and curtailed expenditure to enrich the people; and some dispatched officials to survey farmland and require the people to cultivate it. Although they certainly intended to sustain the people, the well-field system was not restored, and private engrossment of land continued unchecked; field boundaries were not properly established, and state exactions knew no bounds. Could such means of sustaining the people enable everyone to secure a full livelihood? Some honored teachers and tutors, visiting the imperial school and bowing to the elders; some summoned eminent Confucian scholars in great numbers and increased student enrollment; some placed the Six Schools under directors [?]; and some enrolled students in the Three Halls. Although they certainly intended to educate, their personal practice fell short, and schools were not established everywhere; literary expression was prized, while methods of education remained inadequate. Could such means of educating the people enable everyone to recover their innate moral nature fully? The Han, Tang, and Song could achieve only this much in educating and sustaining the people. To ensure that not a single person failed to find a proper place was therefore difficult indeed. Could they have avoided falling short of the responsibility of the principal heir of the lineage? Now, the rulers of Tang and Yu and the Three Dynasties, and those of the Han, Tang, and Song, shared this same responsibility as principal heirs of the lineage and alike implemented institutions and governmental commands, yet the results of their government were so…

title: 弘治三年進士登科錄
text:
不同者是豈無其自耶堯則其仁如天舜則其德好
生禹則不距朕行湯則克寬克仁武王則大賚四海
而皆能體天地之仁也其心既仁故其視天下之飢
寒猶一家之飢寒視天下之昏愚猶一家之昏愚必
欲斯民盡安而後已其治效之盛宜矣漢之君雜於
霸霸則其心不能無偽唐之君雜於夷夷則其心不
能無邪宋之君虛文是尚則其心亦不免於理欲之
雜糅而於天地之仁固皆不能體也其心既有未仁
則一膜之外將為胡越制度雖詳不過維持治安之
具政令雖設不過粉飾太平之規而於民之不能盡
===
安不甚恤矣治不古若豈可歸諸世道之降哉夫為
天地之子而不能體天地之仁則性分之理終有未
盡而吾儒之道終有所歉也是以子思論君子致中
和之效必至於位天地育萬物而後為至蓋萬物一
原而位育之效乃君子之所必至者使天地有一之
未位萬物有一之未育則我之所得於天者能盡充
乎論至誠盡性之事必至於參天地賛化育而後為
全蓋三才一理而參賛之事亦性分之所固有者使
人物之性有所未盡參賛之功未臻其極則天之責
於我者能無負乎得於天者不能盡充而責於我者

妥不甚恤矣治不古若豈可歸諸世道之降哉夫為
天地之子而不能體天地之仁則性分之理終有未
盡而吾儒之道終有所歉也是以子思論君子致中
和之效必至於位天地育萬物而後為至蓋萬物一
原而位育之效乃君子之所必至者使天地有一之
未位萬物有一之未育則我之所得於天者能盡充
乎論至誠盡性之事必至於參天地贊化育而後為
全蓋三才一理而參贊之事亦性分之所固有者使
人物之性有所未盡參贊之功未臻其極則天之責
於我者能無負乎得於天者不能盡充而責於我者
punctuated:
不同者，是豈無其自耶？堯則其仁如天，舜則其德好生，禹則不距朕行，湯則克寬克仁，武王則大賚四海，而皆能體天地之仁也。其心既仁，故其視天下之飢寒猶一家之飢寒，視天下之昏愚猶一家之昏愚，必欲斯民盡安而後已，其治效之盛宜矣。漢之君雜於霸，霸則其心不能無偽；唐之君雜於夷，夷則其心不能無邪；宋之君虛文是尚，則其心亦不免於理欲之雜糅，而於天地之仁固皆不能體也。其心既有未仁，則一膜之外將為胡越。制度雖詳，不過維持治安之具；政令雖設，不過粉飾太平之規，而於民之不能盡安，不甚恤矣。治不古若，豈可歸諸世道之降哉？

夫為天地之子而不能體天地之仁，則性分之理終有未盡，而吾儒之道終有所歉也。是以子思論君子致中和之效，必至於位天地、育萬物而後為至。蓋萬物一原，而位育之效乃君子之所必至者。使天地有一之未位，萬物有一之未育，則我之所得於天者能盡充乎？論至誠盡性之事，必至於參天地、賛化育而後為全。蓋三才一理，而參賛之事亦性分之所固有者。使人物之性有所未盡，參賛之功未臻其極，則天之責於我者能無負乎？得於天者不能盡充，而責於我者
translation_en:
…differed: could this have been without a cause? Yao’s benevolence was like Heaven; Shun’s virtue cherished life; Yu declared, “Do not oppose my conduct”; Tang was both magnanimous and benevolent; and King Wu bestowed great gifts throughout the Four Seas. All could embody the benevolence of Heaven and Earth. Since their hearts were benevolent, they regarded hunger and cold throughout the realm as hunger and cold within their own household, and ignorance and benightedness throughout the realm as ignorance and benightedness within their own household. They would not rest until all the people were secure. It was fitting that their government should achieve such splendid results. The rulers of Han mixed their rule with the ways of the hegemon; thus their hearts could not be free of deceit. The rulers of Tang mixed their rule with the ways of the barbarians; thus their hearts could not be free of perversity. The rulers of Song prized empty formalities; thus their hearts likewise could not escape the intermingling of principle and selfish desire. None could truly embody the benevolence of Heaven and Earth. Since their hearts fell short of benevolence, those beyond the membrane of their own bodies became as alien to them as the Hu and the Yue. However detailed their institutions, these were merely instruments for maintaining order; however well established their governmental commands, these were merely devices for putting a gloss of peace upon the realm. They cared little that the people were not all secure. Can their failure to govern as well as the ancients be attributed to the decline of the age?

To be a son of Heaven and Earth yet unable to embody their benevolence means that the principles inherent in one’s nature remain incompletely fulfilled, and that our Confucian Way remains deficient. Thus, when Zisi discusses the effects of the gentleman’s bringing equilibrium and harmony to their utmost, he regards them as consummate only when Heaven and Earth are established in their proper places and the myriad things are nourished. For the myriad things have a single source, and establishing their proper places and nourishing them are effects that the gentleman must attain. If either Heaven or Earth were not properly situated, or any of the myriad things remained unnourished, could what I have received from Heaven be fully realized? When he discusses attaining utmost sincerity and fully realizing one’s nature, he regards the undertaking as complete only when one forms a triad with Heaven and Earth and assists their transforming and nourishing activity. For the Three Powers—Heaven, Earth, and humanity—share one principle, and joining and assisting them is likewise inherent in one’s allotted nature. If the natures of human beings and other things remained in any respect unfulfilled, and the work of joining and assisting Heaven and Earth had not reached its utmost, could I avoid failing in the responsibility Heaven has laid upon me? If what I have received from Heaven cannot be fully realized, and the responsibility laid upon me…

title: 弘治三年進士登科錄
text:
不能無負不可以言克肖之子也而況任宗子之責
者乎此唐虞三代之君所以無愧於宗子之責而非
漢唐宋之君所能及也然極教養之周而臻位育參
賛之效仁之功用無以踰於是矣是豈一蹴所能及
哉蓋自然而然者性之者也勉然而然者身之者也
欽明文思温恭允塞此堯舜之所以為性之也祗台
徳先聖敬日躋敬勝怠吉此禹湯武之所以為身之
也是雖有性之身之之異而其所以體乎仁者則皆
不外乎敬也然則
今日行之之所自始者又豈外此而他求哉伏觀
陛下嗣登天位三載於茲所以養民者既惟成憲是守而猶
親耕籍田以勸農所以教民者既惟舊章是遵而猶
親幸太學以勸士仁之形於政者如此則
陛下有得於持敬之功宜亦多矣然敬之一言聖學成始
成終之要而仁之功用必厎於極而後無歉於宗子
之責日新之功豈可忽焉而不加之意乎伏願
陛下因其已操者而操之益勤因其已行者而行之益固
未與物接則敬以存養之耳雖未有聞也洞洞屬屬猶
神明之對越目雖未有覩也戰戰兢兢猶上帝之監
臨以至至靜之中亦無不然則天理之公不得以放

之責日新之功豈可忽焉而不加之意乎伏願

未與物接則敬以存養之耳雖未有聞也洞洞屬屬猶
神明之對越目雖未有覩也戰戰兢兢猶上帝之監
臨以至至靜之中亦無不然則天理之公不得以放
punctuated:
不能無負，不可以言克肖之子也，而況任宗子之責者乎？此唐虞三代之君所以無愧於宗子之責，而非漢唐宋之君所能及也。然極教養之周，而臻位育參賛之效，仁之功用無以踰於是矣。是豈一蹴所能及哉？蓋自然而然者，性之者也；勉然而然者，身之者也。「欽明文思温恭允塞」，此堯舜之所以為性之也；「祗台徳先」、「聖敬日躋」、「敬勝怠吉」，此禹湯武之所以為身之也。是雖有性之、身之之異，而其所以體乎仁者，則皆不外乎敬也。然則今日行之之所自始者，又豈外此而他求哉？
伏觀陛下嗣登天位，三載於茲，所以養民者，既惟成憲是守，而猶親耕籍田以勸農；所以教民者，既惟舊章是遵，而猶親幸太學以勸士。仁之形於政者如此，則陛下有得於持敬之功，宜亦多矣。然敬之一言，聖學成始成終之要，而仁之功用必厎於極，而後無歉於宗子之責。日新之功，豈可忽焉而不加之意乎？伏願陛下因其已操者而操之益勤，因其已行者而行之益固。未與物接，則敬以存養之。耳雖未有聞也，洞洞屬屬，猶神明之對越；目雖未有覩也，戰戰兢兢，猶上帝之監臨。以至至靜之中，亦無不然，則天理之公不得以放
translation_en:
…cannot avoid failing in those obligations, one cannot be called a son who worthily resembles his father—how much less one who bears the responsibilities of the principal heir? This is why the rulers of Tang, Yu, and the Three Dynasties fulfilled the responsibilities of the principal heir without cause for shame, attaining what the rulers of the Han, Tang, and Song could not. Yet when instruction and nurture are made fully comprehensive, bringing Heaven and Earth into their proper places, nourishing all things, and assisting their transformation and growth, the efficacy of benevolence can go no further. Could this possibly be attained in a single bound? Those who achieve it spontaneously possess it by nature; those who achieve it through effort embody it through personal cultivation. “Reverent, discerning, accomplished, thoughtful, mild, and respectful, with these qualities truly pervading them”: this describes how Yao and Shun possessed it by nature. “Reverently, I put virtue first”; “His sagely reverence advanced daily”; and “When reverence overcomes indolence, there is good fortune”: these describe how Yu, Tang, and Wu embodied it through personal cultivation. Although there is this distinction between possessing it by nature and embodying it through cultivation, the means by which they gave substance to benevolence never lay outside reverence. Where, then, should its practice begin today, if not here?
I humbly observe that three years have now passed since Your Majesty succeeded to Heaven’s throne. In nurturing the people, you have upheld established institutions, yet have also personally plowed the imperial ritual field to encourage agriculture. In instructing the people, you have followed established ordinances, yet have also personally visited the Imperial University to encourage scholars. Since benevolence finds such expression in your government, Your Majesty must already have gained much through the practice of maintaining reverence. Yet this single word, reverence, is the essential principle that carries the learning of the sages from beginning to completion. Only when the efficacy of benevolence reaches its utmost extent can the responsibilities of the principal heir be fulfilled without deficiency. How could the work of daily self-renewal be neglected or left unattended? I humbly wish that Your Majesty would hold ever more diligently to what you already uphold, and practice ever more firmly what you already carry out. Before coming into contact with external things, preserve and nourish the mind through reverence. Though your ears have yet to hear anything, remain profoundly reverent and intent, as though in the presence of spiritual powers. Though your eyes have yet to see anything, remain cautious and apprehensive, as though the Lord on High were watching over you. Let this hold even in the utmost stillness; then the impartial principle of Heaven cannot be allowed to slip away…

title: 弘治三年進士登科錄
text:
失於外而仁即此靜時而在矣一與物接則敬以省
察之細微之事易忽也必致其謹有若十目之所指
幽暗之中易忽也必致其謹有若十手之所視以至
應物之際亦無不然則人欲之私不得以滋長於中
而仁即此動時而在矣動靜交養內外不違會萬理
於一原散一理於萬事由利而安由勉而熟由身之
而至於性之之地則
陛下之仁真能體天地之仁也將見一心之中包含萬類
即天地之至大周徧九有即天地之至公經緯萬化
即天地之至正不獨中國在所親也戎夷蠻狄之人
===
孰非一體之親不獨吾人在所愛也鳥獸草木之彙
孰非一氣之愛流通於禮樂刑政之間者自有以浹
人之肌膚敷布於制勅誥詔之表者自有以淪人之
骨髓家給人足之樂雖深山窮谷而不殊讓畔讓路
之俗雖遐陬僻壤而不異雨暘時若海嶽効靈麒麟
鳳凰之呈祥醴泉芝草之貢瑞而位育參贊之效並
臻其極則
陛下之得於天者無一不充天之責於
陛下者無一不盡信足以比隆於帝王矣尚何宗子之責
之有愧哉然此亦充乎固有之性盡其當然之責初

失於外，而仁即此靜時而在矣。一與物接，則敬以省察之。細微之事易忽也，必致其謹，有若十目之所指；幽暗之中易忽也，必致其謹，有若十手之所視。以至應物之際，亦無不然，則人欲之私不得以滋長於中，而仁即此動時而在矣。動靜交養，內外不違，會萬理於一原，散一理於萬事，由利而安，由勉而熟，由身之而至於性之之地，則陛下之仁真能體天地之仁也。將見一心之中包含萬類，即天地之至大；周徧九有，即天地之至公；經緯萬化，即天地之至正。不獨中國在所親也，戎夷蠻狄之人，孰非一體之親？不獨吾人在所愛也，鳥獸草木之彙，孰非一氣之愛？流通於禮樂刑政之間者，自有以浹人之肌膚；敷布於制勅誥詔之表者，自有以淪人之骨髓。家給人足之樂，雖深山窮谷而不殊；讓畔讓路之俗，雖遐陬僻壤而不異。雨暘時若，海嶽効靈，麒麟鳳凰之呈祥，醴泉芝草之貢瑞，而位育參贊之效並臻其極，則陛下之得於天者無一不充，天之責於陛下者無一不盡，信足以比隆於帝王矣。尚何宗子之責之有愧哉？

然此亦充乎固有之性，盡其當然之責，初
translation_en:
…be lost outwardly, and benevolence will be present precisely in this state of stillness. Once you come into contact with things, use reverence to examine yourself. Small matters are easily neglected: exercise the utmost care, as though ten eyes were pointing at you [?]. In darkness and obscurity, vigilance is easily neglected: exercise the utmost care, as though ten hands were watching you [?]. Let this hold equally in every encounter with things. Then selfish human desires cannot grow within, and benevolence will be present precisely in this state of activity. Nurture activity and stillness together, allowing no divergence between the inner and the outer; unite the myriad principles in a single source and extend the single principle throughout the myriad affairs. Advance from acting for the benefit of goodness to resting at ease in it, from strenuous effort to practiced mastery, and from embodying goodness in your person to the state in which it is your very nature. Then Your Majesty’s benevolence will truly embody the benevolence of Heaven and Earth.

We shall then see your single heart embrace all kinds of beings, matching the supreme vastness of Heaven and Earth; extend throughout the nine regions, matching their supreme impartiality; and order the myriad transformations, matching their supreme rectitude. Your kinship will embrace more than the people of the Central Realm: among the Rong, Yi, Man, and Di peoples, who is not kin within a single body? Your love will embrace more than humankind: among birds, beasts, plants, and trees, what does not share in the love arising from a single vital force? What flows through rites, music, punishments, and government will naturally permeate people’s very skin; what is spread abroad in the outward expression of imperial decrees, commands, proclamations, and edicts will naturally penetrate their very marrow. The joy of well-provisioned households and people with enough to live on will be the same even in deep mountains and remote valleys. The custom of yielding field boundaries and giving way on the road will be the same even in distant corners and secluded districts. Rain and sunshine will arrive in their proper seasons; seas and mountains will manifest their numinous powers. Qilin and phoenixes will appear as auspicious signs, and sweet springs and numinous fungi will offer favorable omens. The achievements of setting Heaven and Earth in their proper places, nurturing all beings, and assisting the transforming work of Heaven and Earth will together reach their utmost fulfillment. Then everything Your Majesty has received from Heaven will be fully developed, and every responsibility Heaven has laid upon Your Majesty will be fully discharged. Truly, you will be worthy of matching the greatness of the ancient emperors and kings. How could there remain any cause for shame concerning your responsibility as Heaven’s principal heir?

Yet this too is simply to fulfill your inherent nature and discharge your rightful responsibility; from the outset …

text:
未嘗有所增益而不如此則不足以謂之體仁不足
以謂之宗子雖孳孳圖治必不能大有所為也申生
有言為治不在多言顧力行何如耳盖言之非艱行
之惟艱言而不能行之則亦徒言而無益於治矣臣
謹以力行一言為
陛下獻瀆冒
天威不勝恐懼戰慄之至臣謹對
alt_text:
未嘗有所增益而不如此則不足以謂之〔體〕〔仁〕不足
以謂之宗子雖孳孳圖治必不能大有所為也申生
有言為治不在多言顧力行何如耳蓋言之非艱行
之惟艱言而不能行之則亦徒言而無益於治矣〔臣〕
謹以力行一言為
陛下獻瀆冒
天威不勝恐懼戰慄之至〔臣〕謹對
punctuated: 未嘗有所增益，而不如此，則不足以謂之體仁，不足以謂之宗子。雖孳孳圖治，必不能大有所為也。申生有言：「為治不在多言，顧力行何如耳。」盖言之非艱，行之惟艱；言而不能行之，則亦徒言而無益於治矣。臣謹以力行一言為陛下獻。瀆冒天威，不勝恐懼戰慄之至。臣謹對。
translation_en: …there has never been any addition to what was already inherent. Yet without acting thus, one cannot be said to embody benevolence or to fulfill the role of the lineage heir. Even if one strives diligently for good government, one will certainly be unable to accomplish anything great. Shen Sheng [?] said: “Governing does not depend on many words; it depends only on how earnestly one puts them into practice.” For speaking is not difficult; putting words into practice is what is difficult. If one speaks but cannot act accordingly, these are merely empty words, of no benefit to government. Your servant respectfully offers Your Majesty this single counsel: earnest practice. Having presumptuously offended Your heavenly majesty, I am overcome with fear and trembling. Your servant respectfully submits this reply.
